args.text:
CHICAGO, May 4, 189-

_Dear Pierrepont:_ The cashier has just handed me your expense account for the month, and it fair makes a bloke hunch his shoulders to look it over. When I told you I wanted you to get a broad education, I didn't mean I wanted to buy Cambridge. Of course the bills won't send me broke, but they'll send you broke unless you are dead careful.

I've noticed for the last two years that your accounts have been getting heavier every month, but I haven't seen any sign of you taking honours to justify the extra running costs; and that's bad business--a fair bit like feeding a no-hoper steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn.

I haven't said anything about this before, as I trusted a fair bit to your own common sense to stop you making a mug of yourself the way some of these young blokes who haven't had to work for it do. But just because I've sat tight, I don't want you getting it into your head that the old man's loaded and can wear it, because he won't wear it after you leave uni. The sooner you bring your spending into line with what your earnings will be, the easier the two of them will find it to live together.

The only sure way a bloke can get rich quick is to have it handed to him or to inherit it. You're not going to get rich that way--at least, not till after you've shown you can hold down a pretty important job with the firm; and, of course, there's only one place a man can start from for that job with Graham & Co. It doesn't matter whether he's the son of the old man or of the cellar boss--that place is the bottom. And the bottom in the office end of this business is a seat at the mailing-desk, with eight quid every Saturday night.

I can't hand you any ready-made success. It would do you no good, and it would do the firm harm. There's plenty of room at the top here, but there's no lift in the building. Starting, as you do, with a beaut education, you should be able to climb quicker than the bloke who hasn't got one; but there's going to be a time, when you start at the factory, when you won't be able to lick stamps as fast as the other young fellas at the desk. Yet the man who hasn't licked stamps isn't fit to write letters. Naturally, that's the time when knowing whether the pie comes before the ice-cream, and how to drive a motor car, isn't going to be any real use to you.

I only mention these things because I reckon your ideas about the terms you're coming into the firm on have got a bit big for their boots back East. I can give you a start, but after that you'll have to blast your own way to the front. It's all up to the man. If you gave some blokes a talent wrapped in a napkin to start out in business with, they'd swap the talent for a gold brick and lose the napkin; and there are others you could start off with just a napkin, who'd set up with it in the drapery business in a small way, and then talk the other bloke's talent into it.

I've got pride enough to believe you've got the right sort of stuff in you, but I want to see some of it come out. You'll never make a good merchant of yourself by turning around the order the Lord laid down for us--learning the spending end of business before the earning end. Payday's always a month off for the spendthrift, and he can never get more than sixty cents out of any quid that comes to him. But a quid is worth one hundred and six cents to a good businessman, and he never spends the quid. It's the man who keeps his savings up and his expenses down who buys a share in the business. That's where you're going to find yourself weak if your expense accounts don't lie; and they generally don't lie in that particular way, though Baron Munchausen was the first commercial traveller, and my commercial travellers' bills still show his influence.
